power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objectives: Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is a non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic arterial disease characterized by multifocal arterial beading that predominantly affects women.
Although FMD commonly involves the renal and carotid arteries, its relationship with acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) remains poorly understood.
We investigated the proportion of patients with FMD among patients with ATAAD, focusing on sex-based differences.
Patients aged ≤70 years with ATAAD and ECG-triggered aortic CT angiography (CTA) were consecutively included in this retrospective single-center study.
FMD was defined as multifocal arterial beading ("string-of-beads" appearance) in at least one vascular territory, according to international consensus criteria.
The highest-quality CTA examination was evaluated by an experienced cardiovascular radiologist.
All suspected FMD cases were independently reviewed by a second experienced cardiovascular radiologist, with the final diagnosis established by consensus.
Proportions were reported with 95% confidence intervals and compared between sexes.
Of 214 patients screened, 200 were included (138 men and 62 women).
FMD was confirmed in 18/200 patients (9%; 95% CI, 6-14%), none of whom had a prior FMD diagnosis.
FMD was more frequent in women (12/62, 19%; 95% CI, 11-31%) than men (6/138, 4%; 95% CI, 2-9%; P<0.001).
text.formatted: FMD was more frequent in women (12/62, 19%; 95% CI, 11-31%) than men (6/138, 4%; 95% CI, 2-9%; P<0.001).

text.text: FMD predominantly involved the renal arteries.
Additional carotid CTA was available in 49/200 patients (25%) and in 7/18 patients with FMD (39%); three of these seven patients had carotid FMD.
FMD was observed in a substantial proportion of patients presenting with ATAAD, particularly women.
These findings suggest that FMD is an underrecognized vascular phenotype in patients with ATAAD.
The proportion of patients with fibromuscular dysplasia among those presenting with acute type A aortic dissection remains poorly understood, particularly regarding sexbased differences.
Fibromuscular dysplasia was identified on CT angiography in 19% of women and 4% of men with acute type A aortic dissection (9% overall).
Fibromuscular dysplasia represents an underrecognized vascular phenotype in patients with acute type A aortic dissection, particularly women.
Its coexistence with connective tissue disease highlights the heterogeneity of this patient population.
Acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) is a life-threatening cardiovascular emergency.

The global incidence of aortic dissection is estimated at 3-6 cases per 100,000 personyears, with ATAAD accounting for nearly two-thirds of cases.[ 1; 2] Despite advances in diagnostic and surgical techniques, ATAAD continues to carry a 30-day mortality exceeding 20%. [3] Prompt surgical repair remains the standard of care; however, outcomes are influenced by patient age, hemodynamic status, and institutional experience. [4] [5] [6] Sex differences in presentation and outcomes have been increasingly recognized.

text.text: Women are typically older at ATAAD presentation and are more likely to exhibit atypical symptoms. [7] Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is a non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic disease affecting arterial vessel walls.

text.text: Arterial manifestations include beading, stenosis, aneurysms, tortuosity, and dissections.
The most common subtype of FMD presents with a "string-of-beads" appearance.

FMD most commonly affects the renal and carotid arteries, but other arteries can also be affected.[ 8; 9] Clinical manifestations of FMD include hypertension, headache, and pulsatile tinnitus, but FMD can also be asymptomatic. [10] The exact prevalence of FMD remains uncertain.

text.text: However, data from potential kidney donors undergoing CTA suggest an overall prevalence of 2.6-2.8%, with a higher prevalence among women (approximately 3.9%) than among men (1.2%). [11; 12] When invasive angiography was used to detect FMD in potential kidney donors, a prevalence of 4.4% was reported.[ 13] However, these prevalence estimates may be influenced by selection bias, because potential kidney donors are typically younger, healthier, and largely asymptomatic compared with patients with ATAAD. [11] Hendricks et al. showed that in an older population with hypertension and a higher burden of atherosclerosis, the prevalence of FMD was 5.8%, higher than the 2.3% prevalence observed in the potential kidney donor comparison group in that study. [14] Although traditionally considered a disease mainly affecting medium-sized vessels, FMD has recently been associated with changes in the thoracic aorta.

text.text: A cohort study reported that patients with FMD had slightly larger diameters of the ascending aorta compared with age-and sex-matched controls.[ 15] Case reports have described ATAAD in patients with FMD.[ 16; 17] However, the proportion of patients with ATAAD who have FMD has not been systematically investigated, and potential sex-based differences remain unknown.
Therefore, the aim of this cross-sectional analysis was to determine the proportion of 111 FMD among patients aged ≤70 years with ATAAD and to evaluate sex-based 112 differences.
The study was approved by the institutional review board of Erasmus MC, which waived the requirement for informed consent because of the retrospective nature of the study.
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and applicable institutional and national regulations.
We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study including patients aged 18-70 years who were surgically treated for ATAAD at Erasmus Medical Center (EMC) between 2007 and 2024.

We restricted the analysis to patients ≤70 years of age because we hypothesized that the association between FMD and ATAAD would be more apparent in a younger population, in whom competing vascular pathologies such as atherosclerosis are less prevalent.
Patients were eligible for inclusion if they had a confirmed diagnosis of ATAAD and an available diagnostic ECG-triggered CT angiography (CTA) of the entire aorta.
When multiple CTA examinations were available, the examination with the highest image quality was selected for analysis.
All scans were reviewed by a radiologist (AC, with 12 years of experience in cardiovascular imaging).
Cases suspected of FMD were independently reviewed by a second radiologist (AW, with 20 years of experience in cardiovascular imaging), and the final diagnosis was established by consensus.
All available medium-sized vessels were evaluated for FMD (renal, carotid, vertebral, subclavian, coronary, celiac, mesenteric, and iliac arteries).
When additional CTA examinations of the carotid arteries were available, these were also reviewed for the presence of FMD.
Radiological signs of FMD were assessed according to the diagnostic criteria outlined in the First International Consensus on the Diagnosis and Management of Fibromuscular Dysplasia.

Definite FMD was defined as multifocal beading ("string-of-beads" appearance) in at least one vessel.[ 8] Consistent with the international consensus criteria, isolated focal stenoses or aneurysms were not considered diagnostic of FMD.

Baseline clinical characteristics were obtained from our institution's extended cohort of the SIZE MATTERS study, a multicenter project investigating sex-specific characteristics and outcomes in thoracic aortic disease.

These characteristics included demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and information on genetically confirmed or suspected connective tissue disease. [18] Continuous variables are presented using mean ± standard deviation, and categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages.
text.formatted: These characteristics included demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and information on genetically confirmed or suspected connective tissue disease. <ref type="bibr">[18]</ref> Continuous variables are presented using mean ± standard deviation, and categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages.

text.text: The proportion of patients with FMD is reported with two-sided 95% confidence intervals calculated using the Wilson score method.
Differences in continuous variables were assessed using the independent-samples t-test.
Differences in categorical variables were assessed using the χ² test; Fisher's exact test was used when expected cell counts were less than five.
A P-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
text.formatted: A P-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

text.text: Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows (version 28.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).
In total, 214 patients aged 18-70 years underwent emergency surgery for ATAAD at our institution between 2007 and 2024.
Fourteen patients were excluded due to the absence of diagnostic CTA imaging.
Ultimately, 200 patients with ATAAD were included, of whom 62 (31%) were female.
All CTA examinations were available with a reconstructed slice thickness of ≤1 mm.
Initial screening of the CTA studies identified 22 patients with suspected FMD.

After consensus review by two experienced radiologists, the diagnosis of FMD was confirmed in 18/200 patients (9.0%; 95% CI, 5.8-13.8%), whereas in four patients the initially suspected multifocal beading was considered insufficiently convincing for a diagnosis of FMD (Figure 1).

text.text: None of the 18 patients with FMD had a known diagnosis of FMD prior to presentation with ATAAD.
Separate carotid CTA examinations were available in 49/200 patients (25%), including 7/18 patients with FMD (39%).
Among these seven patients, three demonstrated imaging features consistent with FMD in the carotid arteries.
Of the 18 patients with FMD, 12 were female (Table 1).

text.text: Comparison of clinical characteristics between patients with and without FMD revealed no significant differences in age, history of hypertension, or current smoking status.
Baseline characteristics stratified by sex are shown in Table 2.

Genetically confirmed connective tissue disease was present in 12 patients, including Marfan syndrome (n=4), Loeys-Dietz syndrome (n=2), SMAD3-related disease (n=3), Turner syndrome (n=1), ACTA2 mutation (n=1), and MYH11 mutation (n=1).
An additional seven patients had suspected connective tissue disease without a confirmed genetic diagnosis.
No other significant sex-related differences in baseline characteristics were observed.
Representative examples of renal artery FMD in patients with ATAAD are shown in Figure 3.

text.text: Within the FMD group, two patients were identified with an underlying connective tissue disease.

One patient was a woman aged 56-60 years with Marfan syndrome, demonstrating moderate beading of the right renal artery and typical beading of the internal carotid arteries, findings that are not typically associated with Marfan syndrome.
The second patient was a woman aged 61-65 years with ATAAD carrying pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 and SMAD6 genes.

CTA demonstrated typical beading of the right renal artery, discrete beading of the right external iliac artery, typical beading with an aneurysm of the left external iliac artery, and typical beading of both distal extracranial internal carotid arteries (Figure 4).

text.text: In this retrospective study of patients aged ≤70 years, FMD was present in 9% of patients with ATAAD.
The proportion of patients with FMD was significantly higher among women (19%) than among men (4%).

These findings suggest that FMD may be an underrecognized vascular phenotype associated with ATAAD, particularly in women, and highlight the importance of increased awareness of FMD in this population.

The proportion of patients with FMD in our cohort (9% overall and 19% among women) was higher than the previously reported prevalence estimates of FMD (approximately 3%) in potential kidney donors. [11] [12] [13] However, the approximately 4.5-fold higher proportion of FMD in women compared with men in our cohort was consistent with the female predominance observed in potential kidney donor populations, in which FMD was approximately 3.3-fold more prevalent among women.[ 11] A higher prevalence of FMD has also been reported in older patients with hypertension and a higher atherosclerotic disease burden.

[14] Advances in CT technology and improved spatial resolution may also have contributed to increased detection of subtle multifocal arterial beading compared with earlier studies. [19] This study was not designed to determine whether FMD is causally related to ATAAD.

text.text: Hypertension associated with FMD could potentially contribute to the risk of ATAAD, as hypertension, particularly when untreated, is a well-established risk factor for ATAAD.[ 20] However, no significant difference in the proportion of patients with known hypertension was observed between patients with and without FMD in our cohort.
Whether structural alterations of the aortic wall in patients with FMD may independently increase susceptibility to dissection remains unclear.

Schwartz et al. reported slightly larger aortic diameters in patients with FMD compared with healthy controls.[ 15] However, it is uncertain whether this represents direct aortic involvement in FMD or reflects associated factors such as hypertension.
Identifying FMD in patients after ATAAD may be clinically relevant, as it may prompt assessment of associated hypertension and guide additional vascular imaging.

Current international guidelines recommend screening of the carotid and intracranial arteries at least once after a diagnosis of FMD. [8] Radiologists are well positioned to recognize previously undiagnosed FMD in patients with ATAAD, as CTA is routinely performed as part of the diagnostic workup.
text.formatted: Current international guidelines recommend screening of the carotid and intracranial arteries at least once after a diagnosis of FMD. <ref type="bibr">[8]</ref> Radiologists are well positioned to recognize previously undiagnosed FMD in patients with ATAAD, as CTA is routinely performed as part of the diagnostic workup.

text.text: Careful assessment of the visualized branch vessels may reveal characteristic imaging findings of FMD that might otherwise remain unrecognized.
In our cohort, none of the patients with FMD had a previously established diagnosis.
In the overall cohort, approximately 10% of patients had genetically confirmed or suspected connective tissue disease.
Among patients with FMD, two individuals had a known genetic disorder: one with Marfan syndrome and one carrying pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 and SMAD6 genes.
Both patients demonstrated typical beading of the distal internal carotid arteries.

Although this observation may initially appear counterintuitive, it may reflect a more heterogeneous disease spectrum, in which patients can harbor multiple underlying conditions contributing to aortic vasculopathy.
The genetic basis of FMD remains incompletely understood.

In previous studies investigating FMD patient cohorts and genes associated with genetic aortic disease (including COL3A1, ACTA2, and TGF-β pathway genes), no relevant contributing genetic variants were identified. [10; 21] Future studies investigating genetic predisposition in patients with both FMD and ATAAD may provide further insight into potential shared or overlapping genetic mechanisms.
text.formatted: In previous studies investigating FMD patient cohorts and genes associated with genetic aortic disease (including COL3A1, ACTA2, and TGF-β pathway genes), no relevant contributing genetic variants were identified. <ref type="bibr">[10; 21]</ref> Future studies investigating genetic predisposition in patients with both FMD and ATAAD may provide further insight into potential shared or overlapping genetic mechanisms.

text.text: Sex-related differences have also been described in patients with thoracic aortic disease.
Women tend to be older at the time of diagnosis and more frequently present with tubular ascending aortic aneurysms, whereas men more often exhibit aortic root involvement.
[18] The marked female predominance of FMD observed in our ATAAD cohort may represent an additional sex-related difference in the vascular phenotype of these patients.
This study has several limitations.

First, this was a retrospective study performed in a single tertiary center, which may have introduced referral center bias and limited generalizability to other populations, although this was partly mitigated by the consecutive inclusion of all eligible surgically treated patients aged 18-70 years during the study period.

Second, CTA examinations were performed as part of routine clinical care and were not specifically optimized for the detection of FMD, which may have resulted in underdetection of subtle imaging features of FMD.

In addition, second-reader assessment was limited to cases suspected of FMD during the initial review; therefore, subtle findings not identified during the initial review would not have undergone independent second-reader assessment.
Furthermore, image assessment was not blinded to patient sex, which may have introduced observer bias in the detection of FMD.
However, complete blinding to sex was not feasible because sex-related anatomical characteristics were visible on the CTA examinations.

Third, imaging of vascular territories outside the standard aortic CTA scan range, particularly the carotid arteries, was not available in all patients, which may have influenced the detection of FMD.
Because carotid CTA was available in only 25% of patients, the proportion of patients with FMD may have been underestimated.

Fourth, the relatively small number of patients with confirmed FMD limits the ability to perform more detailed subgroup analyses and may restrict the interpretation of associations with clinical risk factors.
Finally, no systematic genetic testing was performed specifically as part of this study, which limits the ability to explore potential genetic relationships between FMD and ATAAD.
The current findings suggest that FMD may represent a previously underrecognized vascular phenotype in ATAAD, particularly among women.
The presence of patients with both FMD and genetically confirmed or suspected connective tissue disease further highlights the heterogeneity of this patient population.
Radiologists play an important role in identifying previously unrecognized FMD through careful assessment of the branch vessels on CTA in patients with ATAAD.

Future studies should explore the genetic and vascular characteristics of patients with both FMD and ATAAD to better understand potential shared disease pathways and their relevance to the risk of ATAAD.
